scenes.title: Dynamic SQL
scenes.narration: Dynamic SQL is query text that a program builds and executes at runtime rather than writing out in full ahead of time.

scenes.title: When you need it
bullets: Table or column names that are not known until runtime
Building a pivot whose columns depend on the data
Optional filters that switch on and off per request
scenes.narration: You need dynamic SQL when a table or column name is only known at runtime, since those cannot be parameters. It is also the standard way to build a pivot whose columns depend on the data. And it lets you assemble optional filters that turn on or off depending on what the caller asked for.

scenes.title: How it runs
steps: Assemble the SQL text into a string
Hand the string to the engine to prepare
scenes.narration: The pattern is straightforward. Your code assembles the SQL into a string, binds user-supplied values as parameters rather than pasting them in, hands the string to the engine to prepare, and finally executes the prepared statement.

scenes.title: Safe parameterized execution
scenes.code:
-- PostgreSQL: bind values, never concatenate them
EXECUTE
    'SELECT order_id, total
       FROM orders
      WHERE customer_id = $1
        AND order_date >= $2'
  USING p_customer_id, p_start_date;
scenes.narration: Here the SQL text is fixed, and the two user values arrive through the USING clause as bound parameters $1 and $2. The engine treats them strictly as data, so nothing the caller supplies can change the structure of the statement. This is exactly how dynamic SQL should pass user input.

scenes.text: Never string-concatenate untrusted input into SQL — that is SQL injection. Bind values as parameters, and validate or safely quote any dynamic identifiers.
scenes.narration: The critical danger is SQL injection: never concatenate untrusted input straight into the query string. Always bind values as parameters, and for dynamic table or column names, validate them against a known list or quote them with the engine's identifier-quoting function.

scenes.title: Two ways to insert values

left.title: Concatenation (dangerous)
points: User text becomes part of the SQL
Opens the door to SQL injection
One crafted input can dump the table

right.title: Parameter binding (safe)
points: Values sent separately from the text
Engine treats them as data only
Structure of the query cannot change

scenes.narration: Concatenating user text makes that text part of the SQL itself, which is precisely how an attacker injects malicious code and can dump or destroy data. Binding values sends them separately from the query text, so the engine treats them purely as data and the structure of the statement can never be altered.

scenes.text: Use dynamic SQL for structure you can't hard-code, but always bind values and safely quote identifiers — treat every untrusted string as hostile.
scenes.narration: Use dynamic SQL for the structural pieces you cannot hard-code, but always bind your values and safely quote your identifiers, treating every untrusted string as potentially hostile.
